facts.statehood_note: One of the original 13; Virginia ratified the U.S. Constitution on June 25, 1788, the 10th state to do so. Its official name is the Commonwealth of Virginia.
facts.nickname: The Old Dominion (also called the Mother of Presidents)
facts.motto: Sic semper tyrannis (Latin for "Thus Always to Tyrants")
facts.name_origin: The name "Virginia" first appeared in the report of Arthur Barlowe from Walter Raleigh's 1584 expedition. It may honor Queen Elizabeth I of England, the "Virgin Queen," or may be linked to an Algonquian phrase (Wingandacoa) or a leader's name (Wingina) the English heard.

government.legislature: Virginia General Assembly (first met in 1619 as an elected assembly, later called the House of Burgesses; the oldest legislature of its kind in North America)
government.chambers: Senate of Virginia (40 senators, 4-year terms) and House of Delegates (100 delegates, 2-year terms)
government.executive: Governor (4-year term; Virginia is the only state where a governor may not serve two terms in a row). The lieutenant governor and attorney general are also elected every four years; the lieutenant governor leads the Senate and breaks ties.
government.courts: Supreme Court of Virginia (7 justices who serve 12-year terms and choose their own chief justice; they are elected by the General Assembly). Below it are the Court of Appeals, Circuit Courts, and General District and Juvenile and Domestic Relations District Courts.
government.local: 95 counties and 38 independent cities. In Virginia, cities are not part of any county; the U.S. Census Bureau counts both as county-equivalents.
government.constitution: Virginia's seventh constitution, approved by voters in 1970 and in effect since July 1971. Its Bill of Rights grows out of George Mason's Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776).
government.kid_line: "That all men are by nature equally free and independent and have certain inherent rights..." (Constitution of Virginia, Article I, Section 1)

long_ago.about: About 30 Algonquian-speaking tribes along the coast joined under the leader Wahunsenacawh (often called Chief Powhatan), governing more than 150 towns with about 15,000 people in 1607. Women farmed maize (corn) and gathered food, men hunted and fished, and families lived in houses called yehakins made of bent saplings covered with woven mats or bark.
A leading nation of the Powhatan alliance living along the Pamunkey River. The Pamunkey and the Mattaponi are the two tribes that held on to their communal reservations, which they still keep today.
A Siouan-speaking nation of the Piedmont above the fall line. Monacan tradition holds that Natural Bridge is a sacred place, called the Bridge of Mohomny (Creator).

An Iroquoian-speaking people whose name for themselves is Cheroenhaka. In 1650 an English traveler recorded their towns on Stony Creek and the Rowantee Branch of the Nottoway River, in today's Sussex County.
One of the large Tsenacommacah nations along the coast. In 1607 a hunting party led by Opechancanough captured John Smith while he explored that river.

today.about: The first Virginia tribe to win federal recognition (2015); also state recognized since the colonial era, with a reservation on the Pamunkey River in King William County.
Federally recognized as one of six Virginia tribes in the Thomasina E. Jordan Indian Tribes of Virginia Federal Recognition Act, signed into law on January 29, 2018; based in Charles City County.
Federally recognized by the same 2018 act of Congress and also state recognized; based in New Kent County.
Federally recognized by the same 2018 act of Congress and also state recognized; centered at Bear Mountain in Amherst County.
Federally recognized by the same 2018 act of Congress and also state recognized; based in the cities of Suffolk and Chesapeake.
Federally recognized by the same 2018 act of Congress and also state recognized; based at Indian Neck in King and Queen County.
Federally recognized by the same 2018 act of Congress and also state recognized; based in King William County.
State recognized since the colonial era, with a reservation on the banks of the Mattaponi River in King William County.

first_peoples.today_note: Virginia has seven federally recognized tribes and eleven state-recognized tribes. Besides the eight above, the state also recognizes the Cheroenhaka (Nottoway) Indian Tribe, the Nottoway Indian Tribe of Virginia, and the Patawomeck Indian Tribe (all three recognized in 2010).
sites: Historic Jamestowne (Colonial National Historical Park): archaeology shows Native people used the Jamestown site more than 10,000 years ago
Natural Bridge: a sacred place in Monacan tradition
Pamunkey and Mattaponi reservations in King William County, homelands these nations still hold today

history.event: Hunter-gatherers arrive in what is now Virginia; Daugherty's Cave was used as a rock shelter by 9,800 years ago.
In the late Woodland period, farming of corn and squash, and later beans and tobacco, spreads into the region. Palisaded (walled) towns begin around 1200.
About 30 Tsenacommacah tribes unite under Wahunsenacawh (Chief Powhatan).
The Virginia Company of London founds Jamestown, the first permanent English colony, on Powhatan land.

An elected assembly (later the House of Burgesses) first meets. In August, the ship White Lion lands 20–30 captive Africans at Old Point Comfort, the first Africans brought ashore in the English colony. They are traded for food and supplies.
Colonial courts and laws turn slavery into a lifelong, race-based system passed down through the mother (laws of 1661 and 1662).
The Treaty of Middle Plantation makes signing nations, including the Nottoway, tributaries of the colony and reduces their independence and land.

On May 15, the Virginia Convention tells Virginia's delegates in the Continental Congress to propose independence. On June 12 it adopts George Mason's Virginia Declaration of Rights, even though slavery continues in Virginia.
American and French forces defeat the British at the siege of Yorktown; Cornwallis surrenders on October 19.
Virginia ratifies the U.S. Constitution on June 25, becoming the 10th state.
Enslaved Virginians resist: Gabriel (Gabriel Prosser) plans a revolt in 1800, and Nat Turner leads an uprising in 1831. By 1860 about 490,000 people, roughly one-third of Virginians, are enslaved.

Virginia secedes and Richmond becomes the Confederate capital. At Fort Monroe on May 27, General Benjamin Butler refuses to return freedom seekers, and the fort becomes known as "Freedom's Fortress." Northwestern counties stay with the Union and later form West Virginia.
Robert E. Lee surrenders at Appomattox Court House on April 9.

A convention writes a new constitution (1867–1868) that protects the right of Black men to vote and creates free public schools; voters approve it on July 6, 1869, and Virginia is restored to the United States on January 26, 1870. Black Virginians around Richmond, Danville, and the Tidewater build communities, take a greater role in public life, and many buy land.

trailblazers.name: Pocahontas (Amonute, also called Matoaka)
trailblazers.text: Pocahontas was a daughter of Wahunsenacawh, leader of the Powhatan alliance. English colonists captured her in 1613 and held her for ransom; she was baptized as Rebecca and married John Rolfe in 1614. Her story was later romanticized, so teachers should rely on careful histories and Powhatan descendants' own accounts.

trailblazers.name: Booker T. Washington
trailblazers.text: Booker T. Washington was born enslaved on a tobacco farm in Franklin County, Virginia, and lived there through the Civil War. He studied at Hampton Institute and became the nation's best-known Black educator, serving as principal of Tuskegee Institute in Alabama. His birthplace is now Booker T. Washington National Monument.

trailblazers.name: Maggie L. Walker
trailblazers.text: Maggie Lena Walker of Richmond chartered the St. Luke Penny Savings Bank in 1903, becoming the first African American woman to charter a bank and to serve as a bank president. She wanted to help Black families save money and buy homes. Later in life she used a wheelchair and kept leading.

trailblazers.name: Mary W. Jackson
trailblazers.text: Mary Jackson, a native of Hampton, Virginia, worked as a mathematician (a human "computer") at the NACA Langley laboratory and ran experiments in a supersonic wind tunnel. In 1958 she became NASA's first Black female engineer. She later helped children at a Hampton community center build their own wind tunnel.

trailblazers.name: Barbara Rose Johns
trailblazers.group: Black American girl and civil rights leader
trailblazers.text: At 16, Barbara Johns led a student strike on April 23, 1951, at R. R. Moton High School in Farmville to protest crowded, unequal school buildings. The case that followed, Davis v. County School Board of Prince Edward County, became part of Brown v. Board of Education. Virginia now marks April 23 as Barbara Johns Day.

trailblazers.name: Mildred Loving
trailblazers.text: Mildred Jeter married Richard Loving in 1958, but Virginia law then banned marriages between people of different races, and the couple were forced to leave the state. Their case, Loving v. Virginia (1967), led the U.S. Supreme Court to strike down laws banning interracial marriage.

landforms: Blue Ridge Mountains, with Mount Rogers, the highest point (5,729 feet)
Ridge-and-Valley region and the Shenandoah Valley
geography.regions: From east to west Virginia has the Tidewater coastal plain (with the Eastern Shore), the Piedmont, the Blue Ridge Mountains, the Ridge-and-Valley region (including the Shenandoah Valley), and the Cumberland Plateau in the far southwest.

ecosystems.name: Chesapeake Bay estuary
ecosystems.about: The bay is a drowned river valley of the ancient Susquehanna River. It holds clams, oysters, about 350 kinds of saltwater and estuarine fish, and an estimated 238 million blue crabs (2025).

ecosystems.name: Appalachian mountain forests (Blue Ridge and Shenandoah)
ecosystems.about: Oak trees give off a haze that helps give the Blue Ridge its blue color. Black bears (about 5,000–6,000 in the state) live here, and peregrine falcons are being brought back in Shenandoah National Park.

ecosystems.name: Coastal swamps
ecosystems.about: Bald cypress wetland forests grow in the Great Dismal and Nottoway swamps, home to fish like the swampfish and pirate perch.

ecosystems.name: Mountain streams
ecosystems.about: Streams on the Cumberland Plateau and other high regions hold brook trout (the state fish), smallmouth bass, and the Kanawha darter; the Eastern hellbender salamander also lives in Virginia.

science.weather: Humid weather with thunderstorms on 35–45 days a year; tornadoes are most common April to September. Hurricanes and tropical storms can arrive August to October; Hurricane Camille (1969) was Virginia's deadliest natural disaster. Winter storms can bring heavy snow, like 36.6 inches in one day in the January 2016 blizzard. Earthquakes are rare, but a magnitude 5.8 quake struck central Virginia on August 23, 2011.
science.resources: Agriculture is Virginia's largest industry (soybeans, corn, cut flowers, tobacco), and the Shenandoah Valley is its richest farm region. Virginia is the country's third-largest seafood producer (sea scallops, oysters, blue crabs, menhaden, clams); government, military, and high-tech jobs also drive the economy, and coal is mined in the three mountainous regions.
science.highlight: About 35 million years ago a space rock (bolide) slammed into what is now eastern Virginia, making the buried Chesapeake Bay impact crater. Scientists think the crater may explain some of the sinking land and small earthquakes in the region.

g3_ss.title: Virginia's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Map Richmond, Virginia Beach, and the student's town; learn the General Assembly (Senate and House of Delegates), the governor, and the Supreme Court; read Article I, Section 1 together.

g3_ss.title: Virginia's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Meet the Powhatan, Monacan, and Nottoway; build a model yehakin; locate the seven federally recognized tribes on a map today.

g3_ss.title: Virginia Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Short biographies and timeline cards for Maggie L. Walker, Barbara Johns, Mary Jackson, and Mildred Loving; students write a "how they changed Virginia" sentence for each.

g45_ss.title: Virginia's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Algonquian, Siouan, and Iroquoian language groups; Tsenacommacah and Wahunsenacawh; Pocahontas through careful sources; recognition of tribes today.

g45_ss.title: Jamestown, 1619, and Colonial Virginia
g45_ss.plan: Jamestown 1607, the 1619 assembly and arrival of Africans at Old Point Comfort, how slavery laws were built, Bacon's Rebellion, and the Treaty of 1677.

g45_ss.title: Virginia 1776–1870
g45_ss.plan: Declaration of Rights, Yorktown, ratification as the 10th state, resistance to slavery (Gabriel, Nat Turner), Fort Monroe's freedom seekers, the Civil War, West Virginia's split, and Reconstruction.

g3_sci.title: The Chesapeake Bay
g3_sci.plan: Where fresh and salt water mix; blue crabs, oysters, and fish; a simple food web and how people protect the bay.

g3_sci.title: Virginia's Mountains and Forests
g3_sci.plan: Blue Ridge and Shenandoah habitats, black bears, dogwoods, and why the mountains look blue.

g3_sci.title: Virginia Weather Watch
g3_sci.plan: Thunderstorms, hurricanes like Camille, and snowstorms; build a weather journal and a family safety plan.

g45_sci.title: The Chesapeake Bay Impact Crater
g45_sci.plan: Meteor impacts, buried craters, and how scientists find them; link to land sinking and rare earthquakes such as the 2011 quake.

g45_sci.title: Estuary Ecosystems and Seafood Science
g45_sci.plan: Salinity, oyster reefs as water filters, blue crab life cycles, and invasive blue catfish.

g45_sci.title: Flight Science at Langley
g45_sci.plan: Wind tunnels and aerodynamics through the work of Mary Jackson; students build and test a simple wind tunnel or paper-wing models.
